extracted.intended_audience: general readers and practitioners of travel writing and natural history (Victorian-era nonfiction readers, naturalists, and geographers)
extracted.subtask_description: Compose a travelogue that combines on-site narrative description with natural-history observation and analysis, organized to make geographical, zoological, and ethnological relationships clear to readers. Emphasizes accuracy of field notes, use of illustrations and maps, and the integration of geological and biological evidence to support larger conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan and state the work's plan up front
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the plan of the work so readers will always know where they are and in what direction they are going.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wallace states his choice of arrangement (geographical, zoological, and ethnological) and explains why a chronological arrangement would confuse readers; include a preface explaining purpose and layout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose arrangement to aid reader orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a geographical, zoological, and ethnological arrangement rather than a strict chronological narrative when chronology would 'puzzle' the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When visiting many places at different times, prefer an arrangement that groups related regions together so frequent references (to groups of islands, animal productions, human inhabitants) are intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide maps and constant spatial references
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a reference to the maps which illustrate the work so readers will always know where they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include maps that correspond to the text; refer readers to them repeatedly to maintain orientation across geographic chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select illustrations that truly illustrate the text
rubrics_metrics.description: Use only such illustrations 'that would really illustrate the narrative or the descriptions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations may be from sketches, photographs, or specimens; choose images selectively for explanatory or descriptive value rather than ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write narrative contemporaneously for accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of the narrative and descriptive portions were written on the spot, and have had little more than verbal alterations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping field notes and composing descriptions while in the field helps accuracy; minimize later fabrication or over-elaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay publication until key scientific work is done
rubrics_metrics.description: Postpone publishing travels until important groups in the collection are named and described and some problems (variation and geographical distribution) are worked out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wallace delayed six years so he could describe important specimens and address scientific questions; sequence publication to ensure scientific value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance factual reporting with theoretical exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapters on Natural History were written 'in the hope of exciting an interest' and sometimes explain views in detail, while in other cases the author confines himself to statements of the more interesting facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide case-by-case whether to present detailed theoretical interpretation or to restrict to compelling facts, depending on complexity and intended audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define scope and boundaries clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the region (the Malay Archipelago) and its limits explicitly, including which islands and groups are included and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give a clear definitional statement for the work's scope (geographic limits, taxonomic focus, temporal bounds) so readers understand the logical frame of discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use interdisciplinary evidence to support claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ geology, physical geography, vegetation, and animal life together to sketch main features and support biogeographical conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate data from multiple fields (sea depths, volcanic belts, species distributions) rather than relying on a single line of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comparative, relatable scales and analogies
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare islands and regions to familiar areas (e.g., 'some of its separate islands are larger than France', 'Eighteen more islands are, on the average, as large as Jamaica') to convey scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where readers may not grasp raw measures, use comparisons with known countries or regions to make extent and significance intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide quantitative data and specimen transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Give explicit numbers for collections and specimens (e.g., counts of bird-skins, Coleoptera, Lepidoptera) and a general statement of what was collected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report specimen counts and disposition (who described them, where deposited) to make the scientific basis transparent and to allow assessment of sample scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure the work into coherent parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide the Archipelago into five groups and follow island chapters with a Natural History chapter for each group, so the work may be divided into five parts, each treating one natural division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a hierarchical structure: parts based on natural divisions, chapters on islands, and group-level syntheses on natural history; this aids navigation and comparative analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base biogeographical boundaries on species distributions and physical data
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw dividing lines among islands based on animal distributions and sea-depth evidence (e.g., distinction into Indo-Malayan and Austro-Malayan divisions using shallow seas and species lists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use presence/absence patterns (elephants, marsupials, particular bird families) together with bathymetric and geological information to justify regional divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use striking local contrasts as illustrative evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlight abrupt transitions (e.g., the Bali–Lombock contrast) as powerful demonstrations of biogeographical boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select sharp, easily described contrasts to make abstract divisions concrete for the reader; provide local examples of differing fauna/flora.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support generalizations with specific historical and numerical examples
rubrics_metrics.description: When discussing volcanoes or earthquakes, give dates, casualties, and concrete effects (e.g., 'eruption of Tomboro in Sumbawa, in 1815, 12,000 people were destroyed').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantiate broad claims about natural forces with documented incidents, dates, and measurable consequences to strengthen credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge contributors and sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Thank and credit those who aided the journey, provided specimens, photographs, descriptions, or logistical support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include explicit acknowledgements (names, institutions, what they provided) to document provenance of material and collaborations.
